title: Fair pay
tomorrow: the set's headed for a dumpster. why does a war law stop for trees?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the week came home to Egypt: you know the heart of a stranger. We were strangers. Newcomers often take the jobs paid last.

Why sundown? Because the Torah says the hired worker is poor, "and setteth his heart upon it." Tonight's groceries ride on today's pay. The Talmud tells a story that pushes further. Porters are hauling barrels of wine for a rabbi named Rabbah bar bar Hana, and they drop them. The barrels split, and the wine soaks into the dirt. He's furious, and he takes their cloaks to cover the loss. The porters go to Rav, the town's great teacher. Whose side will he take?
screen: `WHY SUNDOWN?` → `THE BARRELS SPLIT.` → `HE TAKES THEIR CLOAKS.`

segments.voice: Rav says: give them back their cloaks. Is that the law? Rabbah asks. Rav answers with a line from Proverbs: so that you walk in the way of good people. The cloaks go back. Then the porters speak up: we're poor, we worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. Rav says: pay them. Is that the law? Yes, says Rav, and finishes the verse: and keep the paths of the righteous. Look at what just happened. By the letter of the law, the porters might owe for the wine. Rav reaches past the letter, toward what the verse calls good and righteous, because a day's pay is a day's food. The Torah's own rule is plain. Don't hold back a hired worker's wages; pay them the same day, before the sun goes down. Leviticus adds that the wages shouldn't stay with you all night until morning. Lived today, pay today looks like the sitter paid at the door, not later; a freelancer's invoice paid when it arrives; the kid who shoveled your walk paid before the snow melts. Something to tell a friend tonight: in this Talmud story, a rabbi tells an employer to pay the workers who broke his barrels.

segments.voice: Run through the people you owe, even small amounts: a friend who covered lunch, a sitter, a neighbor's kid who raked the leaves. Pick one. With your next few slow breaths, settle it if you can, or set the exact hour today when you will.
screen: `WHO DO YOU OWE?` · `PICK ONE.` · `SETTLE IT, OR SET THE HOUR.`

segments.voice: Fair pay: paying workers fully and promptly, before sundown, because they've set their heart on it.
The line to keep: pay today, before the sun goes down on anyone's wages. Eight days in.

howItsDone: Jewish law treats paying a worker on time as a commandment; many observant employers and families make a point of paying sitters, cleaners and day workers the same day the work is done.

sources.ref: Deuteronomy 24:14–15 (pay the hired worker the same day, before sundown)
Leviticus 19:13 (wages not kept overnight until morning)
Babylonian Talmud Bava Metzia 83a (Rabbah bar bar Hana's porters; Rav cites Proverbs 2:20)

notes: Deuteronomy 24:15 fragment 'and setteth his heart upon it' quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.

Bava Metzia 83a paraphrased: the porters break the barrels, Rabbah bar bar Hana takes their cloaks, Rav orders the cloaks returned ('that thou mayest walk in the way of good men') and the wages paid ('and keep the paths of the righteous'). Proverbs 2:20 paraphrased in the voice, not quoted. Confirm the summary and the spelling of the rabbi's name.
'By the letter of the law, the porters might owe for the wine' is hedged; the Talmud's discussion and later commentators frame Rav's ruling as lifnim mishurat hadin. Confirm framing.
